newsitem.title: JAPAN: Foreign policy debate dumped as Japan vote nears.
newsitem.headline: Foreign policy debate dumped as Japan vote nears.

text.p: Foreign policy issues such as troubled ties with Asian neighbours have all but disappeared in the run-up to Japan's general elections as a new electoral system forces candidates to focus on issues close to home.
Not even emotional territorial disputes, including quarrels over remote islands with South Korea, Russia, China and Taiwan, have come to the fore in campaigning for next Sunday's polls.

The only possible foreign-related issue that could have raised tempers this election is the concentration of U.S. bases on Okinawa, but even that fizzled out last month when the island's governor backed out of an all-out confrontation with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's central government.

The lack of debate over foreign policy or security issues partly stems from a wide consensus among the main parties about maintaining strong military and economic ties with the United States while strengthening Asian diplomacy in general.
In the background are concerns shared by the main parties, except for the Japan Communist Party, of North Korean brinkmanship and China's emergence as a major military power.
Candidates, who face cutthroat competition in new and smaller single-seat constituencies, say they have no time to dwell on such far-flung themes.

"Under the single-seat system, candidates must talk more about concrete benefits they can bring to the local community," said former foreign minister Taro Nakayama, who is now foreign policy director of Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).

Nakayama, a six-time member of parliament, has distributed a pamphlet explaining in detail how much of the state budget he was able to garner for his district in Osaka, western Japan. He does not touch at all on foreign policy or security themes.
The economic daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said in a recent commentary: "Most candidates have decided that foreign policy and other national-level issues will not win them votes."
There are 300 single-seat districts, replacing 129 mutli-seat constituencies which had each returned between three and five members to the powerful Lower House of parliament.
In the new system, primarily introduced to curb graft, 200 additional members will be chosen through proportional representation for the new 500-member Lower House.

Ironically, the system was designed to foster debate on larger policy issues and root out efforts by candidates to appeal to local voters with promises of "pork barrel" spending. The parties themselves must take some blame, commentators say.

"The platforms of all the main parties are inward-looking," said political commentator Masaya Ito. "There is no talk of the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty, although the two sides are to meet in November to overhaul the guidelines under the treaty."
He added: "The parties have all decided that making an issue out of this could backfire, and so have ignored it."
Ito said foreign policy is often a bargaining tool among parties to form coalitions, which makes it even more difficult for them to commit themselves to rigid stances.
While the parties dwell little on foreign policy in their campaigns, a look at policy platforms shows subtle differences, especially over how to deal with Japan's neighbours.

The LDP angered South Korea, China and Taiwan when it announced a set of election promises saying islands in two separate disputes were clearly Japan's. In the East China Sea, the Senkakus, called the Diaoyus in Chinese, are claimed by China and Taiwan. Takeshima, in the Sea of Japan, is claimed by South Korea, which calls it Tokdo.
A dispute with Russia over islands it seized at the end of World War Two, the "northern territories", also smoulders.

In addition, the LDP said in its written platform that there was nothing wrong with visits to a controversial Shinto war shrine, Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo, which is also at the heart of heated disputes with China, Taiwan and South Korea.
But even then, Hashimoto quickly tried to calm relations by saying the government -- should he stay in power after the polls -- would not necessarily toe the party line.
Only the fledgling Democratic Party has came out with something new -- a vague demand for an eventual U.S. troop withdrawal, the first non-leftist political party to do so since the end of the war.
